#!/bin/bash
# Creates the AWS resources the services expect, inside LocalStack. LocalStack runs every script
# in /etc/localstack/init/ready.d once it is ready, so `docker compose up` ends with these in place.
# Names match processor/src/main/resources/application-local-test.yml.
# LocalStack does not enforce IAM, so no queue policy is set here. Real AWS needs one that lets
# S3 send to the queue (Terraform, out of scope for this issue).
set -euo pipefail

export AWS_DEFAULT_REGION=us-west-2

BUCKET=device-logs-local
QUEUE=device-logs-uploads
DLQ=device-logs-uploads-dlq
TABLE=device-logs-index
ACCOUNT=000000000000

# Queues. The DLQ comes first because the main queue's redrive policy needs its ARN.
# Redrive after 5 receives and a 60 s visibility timeout (ADR 0023).
awslocal sqs create-queue --queue-name "$DLQ" > /dev/null
DLQ_ARN=$(awslocal sqs get-queue-attributes \
  --queue-url "http://localhost:4566/$ACCOUNT/$DLQ" \
  --attribute-names QueueArn --query 'Attributes.QueueArn' --output text)

awslocal sqs create-queue --queue-name "$QUEUE" --attributes \
  "{\"VisibilityTimeout\":\"60\",\"RedrivePolicy\":\"{\\\"deadLetterTargetArn\\\":\\\"$DLQ_ARN\\\",\\\"maxReceiveCount\\\":\\\"5\\\"}\"}" \
  > /dev/null
QUEUE_ARN="arn:aws:sqs:$AWS_DEFAULT_REGION:$ACCOUNT:$QUEUE"

# Bucket, skipped if it already exists so the script can be run again by hand.
if ! awslocal s3api head-bucket --bucket "$BUCKET" 2> /dev/null; then
  awslocal s3api create-bucket --bucket "$BUCKET" \
    --create-bucket-configuration "LocationConstraint=$AWS_DEFAULT_REGION" > /dev/null
fi

# S3 sends an event to the queue for every new object under raw/ (ADR 0017). Setting this up also
# makes S3 send one s3:TestEvent, which the processor deletes without writing a row.
awslocal s3api put-bucket-notification-configuration --bucket "$BUCKET" \
  --notification-configuration "{\"QueueConfigurations\":[{\"QueueArn\":\"$QUEUE_ARN\",\"Events\":[\"s3:ObjectCreated:*\"],\"Filter\":{\"Key\":{\"FilterRules\":[{\"Name\":\"prefix\",\"Value\":\"raw/\"}]}}}]}"

# Index table. Primary key: mac + received_at_type, whose value is "<received_at>#<type>". GSI
# customer-index on customer_id + received_at lists a customer's logs (ADR 0022). TTL on ttl,
# on-demand billing.
if ! awslocal dynamodb describe-table --table-name "$TABLE" > /dev/null 2>&1; then
  awslocal dynamodb create-table --table-name "$TABLE" \
    --billing-mode PAY_PER_REQUEST \
    --attribute-definitions \
      AttributeName=mac,AttributeType=S \
      AttributeName=received_at_type,AttributeType=S \
      AttributeName=customer_id,AttributeType=S \
      AttributeName=received_at,AttributeType=S \
    --key-schema \
      AttributeName=mac,KeyType=HASH \
      AttributeName=received_at_type,KeyType=RANGE \
    --global-secondary-indexes \
      'IndexName=customer-index,KeySchema=[{AttributeName=customer_id,KeyType=HASH},{AttributeName=received_at,KeyType=RANGE}],Projection={ProjectionType=ALL}' \
    > /dev/null
fi
awslocal dynamodb update-time-to-live --table-name "$TABLE" \
  --time-to-live-specification 'Enabled=true,AttributeName=ttl' > /dev/null

echo "init-aws: bucket $BUCKET, queues $QUEUE and $DLQ, table $TABLE ready"

content.text:
Two caveats first:

- **The real lookup isn't built yet.** `CustomerLookupConfig` wires `UnassignedCustomerLookup` in every profile. It never calls herd-device-api and returns "unassigned" for every MAC. So with the code as it is, an outage changes nothing: every row is written as `unassigned`. The answers below describe the design (ADR 0019/0020) and how the existing indexer and poller would handle a failing lookup.
- **The queue defaults are local and test values.** ADR 0023 says production values are set per environment later, and `application.yml` has no visibility-timeout default.

**What phones see:** Nothing. Uploads keep working normally. The upload service only checks headers and writes to S3. The customer lookup runs only in the processor, off the upload path, "so a slow lookup can never delay or fail an upload".

**Messages already queued:**
- A MAC still in the 15-minute cache is indexed normally.
- On a cache miss, the lookup throws `CustomerLookupException` and `RecordIndexer` returns `LOOKUP_FAILED`. `QueuePoller` doesn't delete that message, so it comes back after the visibility timeout and is retried.
- The processor never sends anything to the DLQ itself. The queue's redrive policy does that.

**Unassigned during the outage:** No. "A failed or timed-out lookup is an error that leaves the message on the queue, never 'unassigned'." Only a MAC that no customer owns, where the lookup succeeds with an empty answer, is written as `unassigned`.

**Time to DLQ:** The defaults are 5 receives (`maxReceiveCount` 5) and a 60 s visibility timeout. A message that keeps failing is received at about 0, 1, 2, 3 and 4 minutes, then moved to the DLQ at the next receive, about **5 minutes** after it was first picked up. That's well within a 30-minute outage. So almost every message that misses the cache during the outage would end up in the DLQ. Cached MACs only fail once their 15-minute cache entry expires. The repo doesn't say how messages get moved back from the DLQ after an outage.
